Section 4 is titled 'RESEARCH' and contains subsections like 'Research Questions and Hypotheses', 'Setting and Subjects', 'Procedure', 'Statistical Analyses and Results', and 'Observations on Wayfinding and Evaluations of the Buildings' (pages 86-114).
The study describes specific methods including 'Cards Rotation Test', 'Maze Tracing Speed Test', 'target-reaching task', and 'interviews' (page 96).

limitations: Spatial familiarity cannot be evaluated strictly through subjects’ self-evaluation, because ratings are not objective. People can under- or over-estimate their performances when confronted with the idea of being tested (pages 116-117).
minimum_safe_summary: This empirical case study investigated spatial familiarity as a dimension of wayfinding in two university buildings with different spatial characteristics, using spatial ability tests, wayfinding tasks, and interviews with 146 students. Key findings indicate that environmental factors (complexity, visual accessibility, architectural differentiation, signage, plan configuration) and individual factors (department, class, sex, spatial ability, frequency of visit) significantly affect spatial familiarity and wayfinding performance, as well as the type and number of elements recalled. For instance, the IAED building was rated more complex, leading to more landmark recall, while the GRA building was simpler, leading to more path recall. Males generally scored higher on spatial ability tests, and sex differences in wayfinding errors were more pronounced in the complex IAED building. A key limitation was the subjectivity of self-reported familiarity, which did not consistently predict actual wayfinding performance.
